name: World Eater Brothers
description: You must have heard of the two brothers dreaming of ruling the world. With all their previous plans failed, this time they decided to cooperate with each other in order to rule the world. As you know there are n countries in the world. These countries are connected by n - 1 directed roads. If you don't consider direction of the roads there is a unique path between every pair of countries in the world, passing through each road at most once. Each of the brothers wants to establish his reign in some country, then it's possible for him to control the countries that can be reached from his country using directed roads. The brothers can rule the world if there exists at most two countries for brothers to choose (and establish their reign in these countries) so that any other country is under control of at least one of them. In order to make this possible they want to change the direction of minimum number of roads. Your task is to calculate this minimum number of roads.
input_specification: The first line of input contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 3000) . Each of the next n - 1 lines contains two space-separated integers a i and b i (1 ≤ a i , b i ≤ n ; a i ≠ b i ) saying there is a road from country a i to country b i . Consider that countries are numbered from 1 to n . It's guaranteed that if you don't consider direction of the roads there is a unique path between every pair of countries in the world, passing through each road at most once.
output_specification: In the only line of output print the minimum number of roads that their direction should be changed so that the brothers will be able to rule the world.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 238C — World Eater Brothers [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
